fullarm:
Context from a materials paper:
- Why microscale NiTi deforms by stress-induced transformation in some orientations and by plasticity in others is unexplained
- Comparison axis: compression along [001] versus [112] of the B2 austenite
- Machine ~2 um diameter micro-pillars from grains of the two chosen orientations
- Compress the pillars: three load-unload cycles to 3, 5 and 10% engineering strain, then loading to ~10-13% strain
- Deformation of the [112] pillar is spread over the whole pillar as many parallel traces of a single slip plane
- [112]-oriented pillars are not superelastic: unloading is linear and ~12% of the strain is permanent

Panels:
- F3a: caption: Fig. 3. Plastically deformed micro-pillars ... Mechanical response of an [001]-oriented pillar showing superelastic response and a residual strain of 7.3\%. after deformation

Question: The claim under test says [112]-oriented pillars are not superelastic, with linear unloading and about 12% of the strain permanent. What does the stress-strain curve in panel F3a actually show, and how well does it support this claim?

key.answer_key: Partial support at best: the readable curve in F3a is the [001] curve, not [112]. It shows a transformation plateau starting around 430 MPa, then a strain burst near 910 MPa that carries the pillar from about 5.7% to about 12% strain, and about 7.3% residual strain at the reload arrow (o5).
key.grading: Answer key: the audit ruling on the panel (o5), the graded target for this trace.
